speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And in my reply, I will also cover written Question Nos 43 and 21 filed by Ms He Ting Ru and Mr Yip Hon Weng on the topic of COVID-19, filed for 4 and 5 July respectively, please.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked how we will reduce infection rates of the Omicron subvariant transmission.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We anticipated this wave when we learnt about the subvariants BA.4 and BA.5, which have a significant growth advantage over BA.2.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This wave, however, arrived slightly earlier than the July and August timeframe that we expected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is why we have maintained the indoor masking requirement even when cases were low and stable, in order to moderate the infection rate when this new wave arrives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The high vaccination coverage that we have will also temper the size of the wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To reduce the infection rate further, all of us can play our part: stay at home when we do not feel well, test ourselves regularly, especially if we are meeting people who are vulnerable, or if we attend big meetings or events, such as before coming to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if we still want to reduce the infection rate even further, more stringent safe management measures (SMMs) will need to be implemented.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that means reintroducing things like group sizes, capacity limits and masking outdoors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As the Minister for Health, I can never say we will rule out these steps.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We cannot rule out these steps when we are hit with a serious infection wave but, as far as possible, we should avoid them, especially if we are reasonably confident that our hospital capacity can hold up and that we are determined to live with COVID-19 and continue our journey of endemicity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For this current wave, our assessment is that it will not be as severe as the Omicron wave we experienced earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is because many more of us have gained stronger immunity either through booster shots or recovery from infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will significantly impede the circulation and transmission of the BA.4 and BA.5 viruses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In South Africa, the second Omicron wave, driven by these two subvariants, was approximately one-third of the peak of the previous Omicron wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every country’s experience will be different and unique, but we have good reason to believe that this will be a smaller wave than the last.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we should be relieved that the number this week did not double from last week.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Otherwise, we will be at 24,000 or 22,000 this week.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The key is to ensure that hospital capacity is not overly stressed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And here, we have been relying on two strategies that I will go through today: first, ensure high vaccination and booster coverage so that as many people as possible are protected from severe illnesses, if they are infected; second, ensure that our healthcare institutions and facilities are prepared and able to ramp up capacity, should there be increased admissions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These strategies continue to be relevant for this current wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The most important is for everyone who is eligible to take their first booster or their third shot.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: After several mutations, we now need three shots of vaccines to properly protect ourselves against the Omicron variant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The vaccines were developed in the early days, the wild type – or Alpha and Beta – when you need only two shots.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, they are coming forward, which is a good thing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we urge all our seniors who have not taken your booster shot, your third shot, to do so quickly because it makes a huge difference whether you will fall severely sick if infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have also recommended since March that vulnerable individuals should take a second booster, or your fourth shot.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This includes all persons aged 80 and above, those living in aged care facilities or those with underlying illnesses and are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In recent months, we have stepped up our efforts to remind seniors to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We made regular announcements and have been progressively sending out SMS notifications and reminders to eligible individuals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They can walk into any Joint Testing and Vaccination Centre or participating Public Health Preparedness Clinic (PHPCs) or polyclinic to receive their second booster dose.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Alternatively, individuals can also book an appointment using their notification SMS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Since 27 June this year, we have also been sending out mobile vaccination teams (MVTs) to our heartlands to make it even more convenient for our seniors to get vaccinated and boosted.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will cover a total of 60 sites.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Staff and volunteers from our partners, People’s Association and Silver Generation Office, are also reaching out to our seniors through house visits and engagement dialogues to address many of the queries that our seniors may have.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I also know that many Members of this House have been reaching out, talking to seniors and engaging them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Persons who are recommended to receive the second booster under prevailing recommendations should proceed to do so, even if you have contracted COVID-19 previously.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ideally, an individual should wait 90 days after infection to take your second booster.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, wait 90 days and take your booster.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if you are in a hurry for whatever reasons, we will offer the second booster at least 28 days after your infection.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, please tell your residents, "If you have been infected, it does not mean you are exempted from the booster".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, to be safe, take your booster shot.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second prong of our strategy is to augment and optimise our healthcare capacity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While current international and local evidence show that severity of the Omicron subvariants is not worse, compared to that of the earlier Omicron strains, our hospitals, GPs and other healthcare institutions are on standby to bolster their capacity to prepare for future waves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our hospitals remain ready to ramp up dedicated ICU and isolation bed capacity should there be an increase in the number of COVID-19 patients who require hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Actually, there is and they are already doing so and are now very busy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will make it easier to transfer patients from acute hospitals to CTFs without a significant drop in level of care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our GPs continue to take care of COVID-19 cases within the community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nursing homes are equipped to manage lower risk cases within their facilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To help reduce risk of developing severe disease and hospitalisation, COVID-19 therapeutics, such as oral antivirals, for example, Paxlovid, are made more readily available in primary care and nursing home settings as early treatment, and pre-exposure prophylaxis is available in hospital outpatient settings for at-risk populations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With these measures, the vast majority of cases are managed outside of hospitals, which is appropriate, given the high level of vaccination in our population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, our public hospitals continue to face high demand from non-COVID-19 patients, what we call the "business as usual" (BAU) patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over time, we hope more of our CTFs can be multi-purpose isolation and treatment facilities for both COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have already reconfigured one of our CTFs at Sengkang Community Hospital into this new model and we will explore converting other CTFs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Alongside our polyclinics, PHPCs play critical roles in providing Government-subsidised swabs, COVID-19 vaccinations and oral antivirals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We did not reduce the number of PHPCs earlier because we anticipated a new wave of infection, which did happen.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are now in the middle of this new wave and it will be inappropriate to stand down PHPCs at this juncture.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is in response to Ms He Ting Ru's question.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While we have assessed that there is no need to tighten SMMs for now, we urge everyone to play our part to take the necessary precautions, exercise individual and social responsibility to keep infection rates low, support our healthcare workers and healthcare institutions to weather through this wave.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I also thank the Minister for the very comprehensive reply.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Can I ask the Minister what is the percentage of the recent COVID-19 infections that are caused by the two subvariants BA.4 and BA.5 and whether MOH is considering sourcing Moderna and Pfizer-BioNtech's updated COVID-19 booster shots that can better target the Omicron subvariants?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It started with 3%; then 5%; then 8%; then 16%; then 30% last week and50% this week.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By next week, I would expect it to be 70%, 80%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is clearly a more dominant subvariant, compared to BA.2.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, as the Member pointed out, are, indeed developing bivariant vaccines, which means these target two viruses: the original wild type that started in Wuhan as well as the Omicron variant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Early data does show that these bivariant vaccines elicit a stronger immunity response in individuals who have taken them but it is very early days.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to study the risks and benefits of using such a bivariant vaccine, how to apply it in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But – I should add the very important "but" – do not wait for this bivariant vaccine and hold back taking your booster.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have 60,000 seniors, and also those with health conditions, they are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you have not taken your first booster, you need to take it now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if you are 80 years old and above, living in an aged care facility and vulnerable, you do need to take your second booster now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The current booster, the current formulation works very well in preventing you from falling very sick.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, it was previously reported that there was a wave of manpower leaving the public healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Have we been able to hire new staff to make up the shortfall?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, the number of hospitalised COVID-19 cases has increased over the last three weeks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be a cutting back of elective surgeries in our hospitals on the horizon, due to the COVID-19 situation?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is as compared to the height of the Omicron variant wave earlier this year, where we have about 1,700 hospitalisation cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, about 700 beds, 4% cutbacks in BAU, compared to the height of the Omicron variant, 1,700 beds, 15% cut.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have mentioned earlier, from today's number, we have reason to believe the wave should be near its peak and I hope, from here, things will be better.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The current attrition rate is comparable to what we had experienced in 2019.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In February, there was a slight spike after bonuses have been received.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, otherwise, in the latest number, month-on-month, it is comparable to what we experienced in 2019, pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, it is increasingly difficult to hold on to and to recruit foreign nurses, because, with COVID-19 being a global pandemic, the hiring of nurses is a matter of international competition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The good thing is that, locally, young people's perception of the nursing career is, by and large, a positive one.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am very thankful, actually, that, in MOH and healthcare, we have our fair share of talent.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And when Nanyang Polytechnic, Ngee Ann Polytechnic or SIT open up their courses, it is always oversubscribed, lots of competition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: People cannot get in and they have come to us to appeal to get into nursing courses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, therefore, we must be able to accept that, over time, we have to recruit more foreign nurses from different sources, be able to take them in, train them and, over time, recognising that there is international competition, be able to review their pay and pay them competitively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The good ones, over time, should be able to become part of our community and become PRs, live with their family here, go to the local schools.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is the only way for us, to not just weather through this wave, but, also as our population gets older, the size of our healthcare workforce will have to increase and we have to tap on both a strong local pipeline, as well as foreign recruitment.
